title: Sliced launch + vectorization experiments for paged KV interactions
content:
Purpose:
This note captures experiments exploring a different axis of kernel orchestration for FlashAttention-like kernels when the KV cache is paged. The core idea: instead of large monolithic kernel launches that try to cover many tokens and stall on paged KV I/O, split work into fine-grained launch slices that are vectorized at the warp level and driven by a lightweight coordinator. The goal is to reduce tail latency and improve throughput under mixed hot/cold KV distributions while keeping kernel overhead low.

Background and motivation:
- We frequently see two bad modes when serving long-context generation with paged KV:
  1) Heavy synchronous stalls: a single big attention launch waits for page faults or device-to-device transfers to complete, blocking many active requests and inflating P99s.
  2) Underutilized SIMD lanes: when attention windows are short or token distributions are skewed, large kernels run with low occupancy and fail to amortize launch overhead.
- Prior notes focused on aggressive fusion and large coalesced prefetchers. Here we explore the orthogonal approach: reduce per-kernel working set and rely on very fast microkernels combined in-flight by a host-side slice scheduler. This trades more launches for improved elasticity and quicker fallbacks when KV pages miss.

Key ideas and primitives:
1) Launch slicing: break a single attention pass into N slices along the sequence dimension (e.g., 16-token slices). Each slice is a separate CUDA launch that performs attention for its slice range and emits partial outputs to a small ring buffer. Slices can be processed out-of-order subject to dependency checks.

2) Warp-level vectorization: within each slice, map vector lanes to token channels so the kernel favors register-resident shuffles and avoids wide shared-memory reductions. For small slices, this yields lower register pressure and faster per-token compute.

3) Lightweight slice coordinator: a compact host-side state machine (or a persistent device scheduler block) that issues slices opportunistically based on KV page readiness. If a slice's required KV pages are resident, the coordinator launches immediately; if not, it skips ahead and issues other slices whose pages are ready. Skipped slices are backfilled when pages arrive.

4) Backpressure-aware batching: maintain a dynamic micro-batch window where the coordinator aggregates requests that need the same KV pages; when enough coalescing happens, it issues a combined slice to leverage warps efficiently. If coalescing latency exceeds a threshold, slices fall back to per-request execution to preserve latency SLOs.

5) Tiny fused microkernels: for each slice the kernel fuses softmax compute, key-query projections for the slice, and a compact post-scaling path. The fusion targets minimal shared-memory usage to avoid cross-slice interference when multiple slices run concurrently on the same SM.

Microbenchmarks and observations (RTX A100-ish profile):
- Baseline: single-launch FlashAttention-like kernel, sequence=1024, batch=8, median latency per token layer: ~0.93ms, P99: 5.8ms when KV pages hit; with 10% page misses distributed across requests, P99 spikes to ~24ms due to blocking loads.

- Sliced kernel (16-token slices), coordinator that skips missing pages:
  * Median latency per token layer: ~1.05ms (+13% vs baseline) — overhead from more launches and small kernel inefficiencies.
  * P99 with 10% page misses: ~9.2ms (vs 24ms baseline) — large improvement in tail due to non-blocking behavior and better scheduling of ready slices.
  * Throughput under high-concurrency (100 concurrent streams): measured tokens/sec improves by ~6% because slices allow other streams to utilize SMs while some are awaiting KV hydration.

- Vectorized microkernel variants (lane-packing optimization):
  * For slice size 8 and lane-packing factor 2 (two token channels per warp lane), median token latency improved to ~0.98ms vs 1.05ms. Register pressure grew but stayed within occupancy window with compile-time launch config heuristics.

- Coalescing tradeoff: waiting 600us to coalesce more requests before issuing a combined slice improved compute efficiency by 18% but increased median latency by 9% — useful for batch throughput jobs but harmful for low-latency serving.

Memory and KV interactions:
- Prefetch granularity: the experiment uses page-sized KV fetches (4–16KB) from host-managed staging pools. Sliced launches reduce per-launch resident working set and thus allow more concurrent resident slices on the GPU without exceeding KV memory quotas.

- Eviction interplay: because slices are smaller, eviction can be more targeted (per-cohort slab) rather than full-layer evictions. We tested a "soft-cohort" eviction where slices register in a small bitmap; eviction favors least-recent-slice cohorts, reducing thrash compared to LRU at layer granularity.

Scheduler heuristics and policy knobs:
- Slice size: 8–32 tokens. Smaller slices reduce risk of blocking but increase launch overhead. Empirically 12–16 token slices are a good default for 32k-context-class models on A100-like devices.
- Max in-flight slices per stream: cap to avoid head-of-line; we used 6 as a safety limit.
- Coalescing window: 0–1ms depending on latency SLO.
- Eviction aggressiveness: low/medium/high mapped to target resident pages fraction (70/50/30%).

Edge cases and failure modes:
- Excessively small slices when combined with heavy per-slice bookkeeping can regress dramatically because per-launch startup costs dominate. Keep slice kernels minimal — no large per-slice allocations.

- Out-of-order slice completion requires careful reassembly for dependent layers (decoder cross-attention patterns). We observed correctness pitfalls when slices preemptively updated KV indices; solution: immutable index writes, gather partial outputs then perform in-order reduction on host or a final pass kernel.

- PCIe stalls: if page hydration requires host-to-device transfers, launching many slices increases PCIe queue pressure. We mitigated this by coupling slice issuance with a small IO token bucket to throttle transfers and prioritize slices that already have resident pages.

Implementation notes and quick TODOs:
- Prototype coordinator as persistent thread block in device memory: this reduces host launch overhead and allowed sub-microsecond scheduling decisions in our tests. Implementation sketch in code comment block at end.

- Minimal kernel interface: accept slice_id, token_offset, keys_ptr (nullable), values_ptr (nullable), page_bitmap_ptr, output_ring_ptr. If a required page is missing, kernel returns a compact status and the coordinator marks slice for reissue.

- Add low-overhead telemetry: per-slice timing, page-wait time, and warps-utilization counters. Emit compressed telemetry to host every N slices. Use these signals to auto-tune slice size and coalesce window per model and region.

Recommendations and next steps:
1) Build a small proof-of-concept with host-coordinator issuing slices and a simple page-ready lookahead. Validate correctness with decoder-only and encoder-decoder models.
2) Implement persistent-block coordinator prototype to lower scheduling latency and re-measure tail improvements.
3) Add auto-tune loop that adapts slice_size and coalesce_window per customer workload during warmup.
4) Run extended soak tests with realistic KV churn (mix of hot/cold ranges) and measure P50/P90/P99 against current fusion-heavy baseline.
5) Instrument PCIe transfer queues and test interactions with multi-tenant noise on shared hosts.

Quick sketch: persistent-block coordinator pseudo-comment (for embed in repo):
// persistent coordinator maintains circular queue of slice descriptors in GPU DRAM
// worker thread blocks poll the head and attempt to launch microkernel for ready slice
// if pages missing, descriptor is requeued into a retry bucket with exponential backoff

Concluding note:
Sliced launches with warp-level vectorization represent a complementary lever to our existing fusion-first playbook. They trade a modest median latency cost for large tail reductions under paged-KV regimes and improve multi-stream utilization when page misses are non-negligible. Given our customer SLO distributions (tight P99s for interactive apps), this technique is worth prototyping in the serving-runtime repo as an alternative scheduling mode that can be toggled per-deployment.

Unresolved questions:
- What is the interaction with quantized kernels that use different memory layout for KV? Early tests show layout mismatch is manageable but requires small copy/gather per slice.
- Can the coordinator be made fault tolerant across SM preemption events? Persistent-block plus host watchdog seems plausible but needs test harness.

Notes-to-self:
- add microbenchmark notebook with stable seed inputs and synthetic KV churn generator
- flag PR with basic proto: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/659 (linked above)
- sync with storage team on page-size and eviction API
summary: Draft experiment notes exploring launch-slicing with warp vectorization to reduce P99s when paged KV misses occur. Includes heuristics, microbenchmarks, and next steps.
